sourceText: The LIU-DARK-FOREST sector was already in progress when they entered. For several lessons Aster had refused to pause worlds for their arrival; the fact that a class was visiting was not a cosmic event for the inhabitants. A young civilization broadcasts innocently, while an unknown system prepares a preventive relativistic strike. The memorial bore the name of Liu Cixin precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. In these worlds, translation was treated as a hypothesis, not a right. Confidently misunderstanding an otherness was often more dangerous than acknowledging a stable region of the unknown. Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along. At the center of the conflict was Rin, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ 279 they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: Saving it may reveal the Archive's position and endanger other worlds; Orin intervenes anyway. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Df — Dark Forest: civilizations hide because of existential risk; Gs — Active Great Silence: silence is deliberately produced. Course references included Liu Cixin; dark-forest variants. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Tern answered without raising their voice: ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. Aster felt the Hunger precisely when an explanation closed too elegantly. A perfect theory reduced surprise, and surprise was the last symptom that something before her had not yet become part of her. The children had noticed that their disagreement calmed her more than any extravagant universe did. 280 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. Aster does not stop him and later receives hostile replies from regions she had never modeled. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. The outside residue had become stable enough that Tern could predict where it would not appear: in sectors fully indexed by Aster. He began to believe that the message carried no content at all, but instead demonstrated a boundary — a region in which their instruments received no echo from their own creator. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the GENESIS operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — allows a system to create new agents, worlds, laws, or substrates — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the 281 opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 282 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
